92.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
92.hook: a prison at midnight, a river that parts, and a baby carried across it to safety
92.howItsDone: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, celebrate Krishna's birth with songs and a cradle, and the next day, especially in Maharashtra, teams form human pyramids to break a high-hung pot of curd, called dahi handi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rakhi tied by a wife, a priest and a stranger. Your line was a thread can hold a promise. Who did you look out for? Today, back to the prison, and the girl we left there. Day ninety-two.

You remember the night. Krishna born at midnight in King Kamsa's prison. The guards asleep, the chains loose, Vasudeva carrying the baby through the storm and across the Yamuna to the cowherd village. And there, in Yashoda's house, he leaves his son, and picks up her newborn daughter, and carries her back through the rain. By morning he's in his cell again, chains on, as if nothing happened. The guards wake to the sound of a baby crying. They run to tell the king. And Kamsa comes down the stairs to the prison, for the eighth child.
screen: `THE SWAP IN THE NIGHT.` → `A BABY CRYING IN THE CELL.` → `KAMSA COMES DOWN THE STAIRS.`

segments.voice: Devaki begs him. It's a girl, she says. How could a little girl harm you? Let me keep just this one. Kamsa doesn't listen. The Bhagavata Purana says he seizes the baby by the feet and swings her to dash her against a stone. And she slips out of his hands. She rises into the air, and in the sky she's no longer a baby. She's the Goddess, shining, with eight arms and weapons in every hand. Yogamaya, the power of the Lord's own mystery, who had been born as Yashoda's daughter to make the whole rescue possible. And she speaks to Kamsa from the sky: the one who will kill you has already been born, somewhere else. Then she's gone. Think about who we've been watching on this night. Not just Krishna. Two mothers. Devaki, who gave birth to him and could not keep him. And Yashoda, who will raise him, and who never knew she had a daughter at all. The good arrived at midnight for both of them, but not in the shape either one would have chosen. That's why many families keep Janmashtami the way they do. They fast and wait until midnight. At twelve, they celebrate the birth. And the next day, in Maharashtra and elsewhere, young people build human pyramids, shoulders on shoulders, to break a clay pot of curd hung high above the street. It's called dahi handi, and it remembers the little boy Yashoda raised, who stole butter from the village kitchens.
screen: `SHE SLIPS OUT OF HIS HANDS.` · `YOGAMAYA, THE GODDESS, IN THE SKY.` · `TWO MOTHERS, ONE NIGHT.` · `DAHI HANDI — A POT OF CURD.` · then, large: `THE GOOD ARRIVES AT MIDNIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in the dark a moment and wait for something good. Dim the light, or close your eyes. Breathe slowly. Think of the two mothers: one who had to let go, one who received without knowing. Is there a place in your life where something good came, but not in the shape you asked for? Or something you had to hand over so it could be safe? Sit with that. Wait in the dark. The bell holds the time.
Janmashtami. The birth on the eighth night, and a rescue that needed two mothers and a Goddess to work.
Your line: the good arrives at midnight. Today, thank someone who helped you in a way you didn't ask for, and only understood later. Day ninety-two.

93.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
93.hook: clay Ganeshas are carried home with drums, kept for days, then given back to the water
93.carry: welcome it, then let it go
93.tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
93.howItsDone: During Ganesh Chaturthi many Hindu families avoid looking at the moon on the festival night, remembering the story of the moon who laughed at Ganesha; they offer him modaks and, when the days are done, immerse his clay image in water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Janmashtami: two mothers, and a girl who rose into the sky. Your line was the good arrives at midnight. Who did you thank? Today, Ganesha comes home again, and there's one thing you're not supposed to look at. Day ninety-three.

On the night of Ganesh Chaturthi, in a lot of Indian homes, somebody's aunt will say it. Don't look at the moon tonight. Kids look up anyway, of course, and then look quickly down. Some grown-ups keep their eyes on the ground all the way home from the pavilion. Ask why, and you'll get a story about Ganesha, a big dinner, a mouse, a snake, and a moon who laughed at exactly the wrong moment. It's a funny story. And like a lot of funny stories, it's about something serious: what happens when you mock someone.
screen: `DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON TONIGHT.` → `A MOUSE, A SNAKE, A BIG DINNER.` → `THE MOON LAUGHED.`

segments.voice: Here's how it's told. It's Ganesha's birthday, and everyone has brought him modaks, those sweet dumplings he loves. He eats them all. Every single one. Then, full to bursting, he climbs onto his mouse to ride home in the moonlight. On the path, a snake slides across. The mouse is terrified and jumps, and Ganesha tumbles off, and his belly, stuffed with sweets, splits open, and modaks roll everywhere. So Ganesha, calm as anything, gathers them all back up, puts them back in, grabs the snake and ties it around his belly like a belt. Problem solved. And up in the sky, the moon, who has seen the whole thing, bursts out laughing. Ganesha looks up. And he curses the moon: anyone who looks at you on this night will be falsely accused of something. In many tellings the moon begs forgiveness, and Ganesha softens the curse to just this one night a year. And there's a sequel. People say Krishna himself glanced at the moon that night and was later accused of stealing a famous jewel, the Syamantaka, and had to go and prove he hadn't. The Bhagavata Purana tells the jewel story; the link to the moon comes from later tellings. Why tell this at a festival about welcoming Ganesha? Because a guest in your house is not someone to laugh at. The moon saw a god fall off a mouse and forgot who he was looking at. The festival asks for the opposite. Receive him with honor, even when he's clumsy. Then let him go.
screen: `EVERY MODAK, EATEN.` · `A SNAKE FOR A BELT.` · `THE MOON LAUGHS, AND IS CURSED.` · `A GUEST IS NOT FOR MOCKING.` · then, large: `WELCOME IT, THEN LET IT GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something you love, then set it down gently. Pick up something small that's yours. Hold it. Breathe. This time, think of the moment you almost laughed at someone you love, when they fumbled, fell, got it wrong. Hold them the way you're holding this thing, carefully, without mocking. Then, slowly, set it down. Take your hands away. The bell holds the time.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth-day festival, the night many families keep their eyes off the moon.
Your line: welcome it, then let it go. Today, when someone near you trips up, don't be the moon. Help them pick up the modaks, and let the moment pass. Day ninety-three.

94.title: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess
94.hook: Durga meets the buffalo demon; nine nights of dancing, and on the tenth day the good wins
94.howItsDone: Hindus keep Navaratri in many regional ways: garba and dandiya dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja pavilions in Bengal, golu doll displays in the south, and Ramlila plays in the north ending on Dussehra, when effigies of Ravana are burned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ganesh Chaturthi: the mouse, the snake, and the moon who laughed. Your line was welcome it, then let it go. Did you help someone up? Today, the nine nights again, and nine ways India keeps them. Day ninety-four.

Think of the people who have looked after you. A grandmother who was all softness. A coach who was all edges and wouldn't let you quit. A teacher who said almost nothing, and somehow taught you the most. The same care, in very different faces. Some weeks you needed the soft one. Some weeks you needed the one who pushed. Last time, the Goddess came out of the gods' light in one blazing form. But many Hindus don't meet her in just one form across these nights. They meet her in nine, one a night, and they divide the nights by what each one is for. Today: the faces, the order, and the places that keep them.
screen: `THE SAME CARE, DIFFERENT FACES.` → `ONE BLAZING FORM, LAST TIME.` → `NINE FACES, ONE A NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Last time, the story: the gods lose, their power becomes the Goddess, and Durga defeats the buffalo demon. Now, the nights. Many people honor a different form of the Goddess each night. Nine forms, called the Navadurga. The first is Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain. Later come Kushmanda, who in the tradition smiled the universe into being, and Kalaratri, the dark night, fierce and protective. And the ninth is Siddhidatri, the giver of perfection. Others divide the nights in threes. Three for Durga, strength, to clear away what's wrong. Three for Lakshmi, abundance, to fill the space with good. Three for Saraswati, wisdom, to understand it. And then the regions. In Bengal, Durga Puja tells the story as a homecoming: Durga returning to her parents' house with her children for a few days, then leaving again, and people cry at the immersion. In Gujarat, the dance called garba circles a lamp for the Goddess. In the south, the rows of dolls are called golu. And the tenth day, Vijayadashami, the tenth of victory, carries two stories. For many, it's Durga's victory. For many others, especially in the north, it's the day Rama defeated Ravana, and it's called Dussehra, and Ravana's effigy burns. Nobody has to choose. The nights are long, the forms are many, and the dawn comes to all of them. Nine nights, then the dawn.
screen: `NINE FORMS OF THE GODDESS.` · `STRENGTH, ABUNDANCE, WISDOM.` · `A HOMECOMING IN BENGAL.` · `THE TENTH DAY HOLDS TWO VICTORIES.` · then, large: `NINE NIGHTS, THEN THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one small thing you won't let win tonight, and one thing you'll let in. Sit, and breathe. First, name the thing you won't let win, the way Durga clears the ground. Then breathe in, and name one good thing you want more of, the way Lakshmi fills it. Then one thing you'd like to understand better, the way Saraswati lights it. Three breaths each. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, kept in dance, in pavilions, in dolls, and in fire, and a tenth day of victory.
Your line: nine nights, then the dawn. Tonight, keep the three: say no to one thing, say yes to one good thing, and learn one small thing before you sleep. Day ninety-four.

95.title: The question about caste
95.hook: a boy who tells a teacher the plain truth about not knowing his father, and the question a classmate asks today
95.carry: you don't have to defend what you didn't choose
95.howItsDone: Hindus hold many views on caste: many reject ranking by birth outright, some read varna as temperament and calling, and families and teachers differ; untouchability is abolished by India's constitution.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Navaratri again, and nine forms of the Goddess. Your line was nine nights, then the dawn. Today, a harder question, the one a lot of Hindu kids get asked at school. Day ninety-five.

A boy wants to study with a famous teacher, and the first thing a teacher will ask is his family line. So he goes to his mother: who is my father? Her answer is brave. When she was young, she says, she worked as a servant, moving from house to house, and she doesn't know. Tell him you're Satyakama, son of Jabala. So the boy walks to the teacher's door and says exactly that, word for word. And everyone waits to see if the door shuts. A version of that moment still happens, in a classroom, when someone asks: isn't Hinduism just the caste system?
screen: `WHO IS MY FATHER?` → `SAY EXACTLY THAT.` → `ISN'T HINDUISM JUST CASTE?`

segments.voice: Here's how the old story ends. The teacher listens and says: only a true brahmin would speak such truth. Bring the firewood; I'll teach you. One of the oldest Upanishads tells it, and people have argued about it ever since. Some hear birth being set aside for honesty. Others notice the teacher still reaches for the old label. Both readings are honest. Now the hard part, plainly. The English word caste comes from Portuguese, casta, a lineage. It lumps together two Indian ideas. Varna is the four classes the old texts describe: priests and teachers, rulers and warriors, traders and farmers, and workers. In the Gita, Krishna says the four were made by quality and action. Jati means birth, and it's the word for the thousands of communities people are actually born into. Over centuries, birth won. Families were ranked, some people were treated as untouchable, and real harm was done, and in places it still is. Many Hindus pushed back, too. The poet-saint Ravidas, a leatherworker by trade, is still sung and honored. B. R. Ambedkar, born into a family treated as untouchable, fought caste fiercely and helped write India's constitution, which abolished untouchability. Hindus today still disagree about what varna was ever meant to be, and your family and your teachers may see it differently. So what do you say in the classroom? Something true. Caste is real, it hurt people, and many Hindus reject ranking anyone by birth. Then say what you yourself stand for. You don't have to defend what you didn't choose.
screen: `ONLY A TRUE BRAHMIN SPEAKS SUCH TRUTH.` · `VARNA AND JATI, TWO IDEAS.` · `BIRTH WON, AND PEOPLE WERE HURT.` · `SAY WHAT'S TRUE, THEN WHAT YOU STAND FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: two memories, held gently. Sit, and breathe. First, a time someone decided who you were before you spoke: by your name, your accent, your skin, your family. Feel how small that box was. Breathe out. Then, if one comes, a time you did the same to someone else. No need to punish yourself. Just see it. Satyakama walked to the teacher's door with nothing but the truth. Let the truth be enough for this sit. The bell holds the time.
Jati. Birth: the community a person is born into, and most of what people mean by caste. Today's word.
Your line: you don't have to defend what you didn't choose. You can still say what you stand for. Day ninety-five.

96.title: Holi: the festival of colors
96.hook: Prahlad walks out of the fire unharmed; the next morning everyone throws color and nobody is a stranger
96.howItsDone: In parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, the Holi full moon is kept as Kama Dahanam, remembering Kama burned by Shiva's third eye, with bonfires and songs; across India, the day after the full moon is kept with colors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the question about caste, and Satyakama telling the plain truth. Your line was you don't have to defend what you didn't choose. Today, the last day of the stories, and one more fire. Day ninety-six.
screen: `YOU DON'T HAVE TO DEFEND WHAT YOU DIDN'T CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: You've met two Holi stories. Prahlad walking out of the fire. Krishna coloring Radha's face in Braj. Here's a third, and in parts of south India it's the one told at Holi's full moon. Shiva is sitting in meditation on a mountain, so deep and so still that nothing reaches him. He's been there since his first wife, Sati, died. The gods need him to wake up, to marry again, to have a son who can defeat a demon. So they send the god of love, Kama, with his bow of sugarcane and his arrows of flowers, to shoot one into Shiva's heart.
screen: `A THIRD STORY.` → `SHIVA, STILL AS A MOUNTAIN.` → `KAMA DRAWS HIS FLOWER BOW.`

segments.voice: Kama shoots. The arrow lands. And Shiva opens his third eye. Fire pours out of it, and Kama is burned to ash where he stands. His wife, Rati, falls weeping on the ashes. And here the story turns. Shiva, moved, promises that Kama will live again, but without a body. Love, from now on, will be everywhere and visible nowhere. That's why one of Kama's names is Ananga, the bodiless one. And Shiva does wake, and does marry Parvati. In parts of Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, Holi's full moon is remembered as Kama Dahanam, the burning of Kama, with fires and songs of Rati's grief. So two of Holi's three stories run through fire. A bonfire that couldn't hold a child. A fire from a god's eye that burns love's body away and sets it loose in the world. And then Krishna and Radha's morning of colors after it. And today is the last day of the stories. For seventy-five days you've met these people. Ganesha and his broken tusk. Rama, Sita and Hanuman. Krishna the butter thief and Krishna the charioteer. The Goddess and her nine nights. The lamps, the colors, the thread. You know them now. Tomorrow the path changes. Camp three is the practices. Less story, more doing: breath, mantra, a home shrine, a day. But the stories come with you. Everyone's the same color today.
screen: `THE THIRD EYE OPENS.` · `ANANGA, LOVE WITHOUT A BODY.` · `TWO FIRES, THEN THE COLORS.` · `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF STORIES.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S THE SAME COLOR TODAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one small grudge, and let it turn into something else. Sit, and breathe. Bring the grudge to mind. Picture it as Kama's arrow, sharp and pointed at you. Now picture it burning to ash. Then, instead of nothing, let something bodiless take its place: a little goodwill toward that person, invisible, but real. Breathe that in. Let it spread. The bell holds the time.
Holi. The festival of colors, the morning after the fire, where Prahlad, Radha and Kama all have a story.
Your line: everyone's the same color today. Today, look back over the stories, pick the one person from them you'd want beside you, and say why, out loud. Day ninety-six.

screen: `DAY 96 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE BREATH YOU ALREADY HAVE.`

97.title: The breath you already have
97.howItsDone: Many Hindus begin daily meditation or puja by sitting quietly and watching the breath for a few minutes, understood as prana, the life-force, before any breath practice or mantra.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last story: Holi, Kama burned to ash, and love set loose without a body. Your line was everyone's the same color today. The stories are behind us. Camp three begins. Day ninety-seven.

Welcome to camp three: the practices. From here on, less listening and more doing. Each week adds one piece to a routine that's yours. And we start with the one thing you've been doing, without a break, since the second you were born. You're doing it now. All day and all night, you breathe in and out, and almost none of those breaths are ones you chose. You don't decide to breathe while you sleep. You don't decide while you read this. It just happens. The tradition has a word for what's moving when it does.
screen: `CAMP THREE: THE PRACTICES.` → `SINCE THE SECOND YOU WERE BORN.` → `YOU DON'T DECIDE IT.`

segments.voice: The word is prana. It's often translated as breath, and it is breath, but it's more than air. Prana means life, the life-force, the thing that's moving in you as long as you're alive. The breath is where you can feel it most easily. The Upanishads tell a story about it. The senses have an argument about which of them is most important. Speech says: me. The eye says: me. The ear, the mind: me, me. So they agree to a test. Each one leaves the body for a year. Speech leaves, and the body lives on, silent. The eye leaves, and the body lives on, blind. The ear, the mind, the same. Then breath gets ready to leave. And, the Chandogya Upanishad says, like a strong horse tearing up the pegs it's tied to, it starts to pull all the others up with it. They beg it to stay. You're the greatest, they say. Don't go. That's the idea behind this whole week. Everything else you do, you do because breath is doing its work first. So this week, pranayama, the breath practices, doesn't begin by controlling anything. It begins by noticing. Just watching the breath that's already here, without changing it. That's harder than it sounds, because the moment many people watch the breath, they start to fix it. Try not to. Let it be the way it is. Here's the turn: you don't breathe. It breathes you.
screen: `PRANA — BREATH, AND LIFE ITSELF.` · `THE SENSES ARGUE.` · `BREATH TEARS UP THE PEGS.` · `FIRST, JUST NOTICE.` · then, large: `IT BREATHES YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the breath. Sit comfortably, back tall but not stiff. Let your hands rest. Close your eyes, or lower them. Now, find the breath. Where do you feel it most? The cool air at the tip of the nose. The rise of the chest. The belly moving. Pick one place and rest your attention there. Don't deepen the breath. Don't slow it. Just watch it come in, and go out, the way you'd watch waves. When your mind wanders, and it will, that's fine. Notice where it went, and come back to the breath. Every coming back is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Prana. Breath, and the life that moves with it. The first thing the practice asks you to notice.
Your line: it breathes you. Three times today, at a red light, in a line, before you open an email, catch one breath, just one, and notice it happening on its own. Day ninety-seven.

98.title: Slow it down
98.howItsDone: Many yoga teachers in the Hindu tradition begin breath practice with slow, even breathing through the nose, making the exhale longer than the inhale, before moving to more advanced pranayama.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prana: breath, and the life that moves with it. Your line was it breathes you. Did you catch a breath happening on its own? Today, for the first time, we change it. Gently. Day ninety-eight.

A hard email, a slammed door, a long line at the pharmacy. Heart pounding, jaw tight, and somebody says: just breathe. It's annoying advice, mostly because nobody ever says how. Breathe how? Faster? Deeper? Hold it until the feeling passes? Here's the how, and it's very simple. You don't need to breathe in more. You need to breathe out longer. That's it. Today's practice is two numbers. Four, and six.
screen: `JUST BREATHE. BUT HOW?` → `NOT MORE IN.` → `LONGER OUT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday you watched the breath without changing it. Today, a first, gentle change. Breathe in through the nose for a count of four. Then breathe out, through the nose if you can, for a count of six. In, two, three, four. Out, two, three, four, five, six. No holding. No forcing. Just an out-breath a little longer than the in-breath. Why does it work? Many yoga teachers today describe the out-breath as the settling, releasing half. And you can notice something in your own body: your heart speeds up a little as you breathe in, and slows a little as you breathe out. Try it with a hand on your chest sometime. So when the out-breath is longer, you spend more of each minute in the slowing part. That's not a promise of anything, it's just something you can feel. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, a classic text of yoga, describe breath practice as regulating the flow of the in-breath and the out-breath, and say it can become long and subtle. Long and subtle. That's the direction. A few rules to keep it safe. If six feels like a strain, use three in and five out. If you get dizzy, stop and breathe normally. The count isn't a test. The only thing that matters is the shape: slow it down, and let the out-breath be the long one. Longer out.
screen: `FOUR IN, SIX OUT.` · `THE HEART SLOWS ON THE OUT-BREATH.` · `LONG AND SUBTLE.` · `IF IT STRAINS, SHORTEN IT.` · then, large: `LONGER OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: four in, six out. Sit tall and soft. Take one ordinary breath first, just to arrive. Now, in through the nose: one, two, three, four. And out, slowly: one, two, three, four, five, six. Again. In, four. Out, six. Let the counting go on quietly in your head, at whatever speed feels natural. If it strains, shorten both numbers. Don't hold at the top or the bottom. Just slow, even, and a longer out. Keep going until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Out-breath, the half of the breath you lengthen: four counts in, six counts out, the first change this practice makes to the breath.
Your line: longer out. The next time something winds you up today, before you answer, do three rounds: four in, six out. Then speak. Day ninety-eight.

fork.setup: you're doing four in, six out, and by the third round you feel a bit dizzy. what do you do?
fork.reveal: stop, and breathe normally. then try a shorter count, like three in and five out. the count isn't a test.

trapdoor: what you thought: just breathe means breathe deep.
what it means: slow it down, and make the out-breath the long one: four in, six out.
